text.p: Copper prices ended lower in London and New York overnight on trader expectations of a rise in stocks.
Oil prices rose in New York on a shutdown at a large U.S. refinery while gold prices closed basically unchanged.
Wheat prices firmed in Chicago on India's re-entry into the wheat import market and a lower than expected rise in the USDA's wheat stock forecast.
The CRB Index closed up 1.27 points at 241.76.

Copper prices ended lower in London overnight, but managed a moderate bounce in afternoon trade after initially coming off a high of $2,175 in the morning, while tight nearby spreads remained the market's primary focus.

The other LME metals largely range-traded, excluding lead which trundled up above the $700 level to clinch a strong close. Three-months copper finished the kerb at $2,148 a tonne, down $15 from Wednesday after failing to hold above the $2,150 level. Traders said the strong backwardations had been attracting copper into LME warehouses and they expected stocks to rise on Friday between 5,000 and 10,000 tonnes.

Lead pushed higher on buying throughout the day, in part by delta hedging against call options on the back of earlier Far Eastern buying, traders said. It finished at $700, up $21 and the highest since November 27.

Aluminium finished just $1 higher than on Wednesday at $1,528, close to the centre of the day's range. Nickel similarly finished virtually changed at $6,705, despite an early crumble to a low around $6,660. But weak technicals left it vulnerable to a drop to November 18 low of $6,600, analysts said.
It followed copper off its lows of $1,513.
Copper prices also ended lower in the U.S. as the market expected a hike in the London exchange's stocks on Friday, and continued to monitor tightness in the LME December dates next week.
Most-active March COMEX settled 0.65 cent weaker at 99.70 cents, traded 100.70 to 98.50 cents.
CBOT wheat futures closed higher on news India would import two million tonnes of wheat over the near term, traders said.
"The India news is adding a little more support to the market," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
India's Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said Thursday India will import two million tonnes of wheat in fiscal 1996-97 (April-March) to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.
"The government has decided during the current financial year it will import two million tonnes of wheat," Yadav told the Indian parliament.
Rumors circulated early Thursday that India this week purchased one million tonnes of wheat from Australia.
Wheat futures also found support from USDA's weekly export sales report Thursday which showed U.S. net exports of wheat during the week ended December 5 at 346,200 tonnes.
The market was expecting from 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes.
Prices also were boosted by USDA's minor upward adjustment in world ending wheat stocks for 1996-97 of 530,000 tonnes. There were expectations for a one- to two-million-tonne hike.
Wheat closed 3-1/2 to 6-1/4 cents per bushel higher, with December up five at $4.04.
NYMEX crude and oil product futures edged higher Thursday afternoon as a bounce from recent losses gained momentum on an outage at Tosco Corp's Bayway, New Jersey plant.

In fairly thin trding, January crude futures were holding well within Wednesday's wide range, hitting a high near the open of $23.82 a barrel and holding above a low $23.33. The contract was up 33 cents at $23.72 near the close.

After the sharp losses this week, which sent crude prices more than $2 below last Friday's levels, the bounce Thursday morning was helped by the outage at Tosco Bayway's fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) unit.
An unspecified problem there caused a small fire and sources familiar with company operations couldn't say when it would be back up.
The FCC there is among the largest and most sophisticated in the world, with a rated capacity of 140,000 barrels per day (bpd) out of a total plant processing capacity of 290,000 bpd.
It was unclear what the market impact would be, however, as December looks like being an exceptionally heavy month for gasoline imports, traders said.
New York precious metals futures ended little changed Thursday, as the complex continued to consolidate following last month's slide, but volumes were good for a low volatility day, traders said.

"There's support in spot gold around $368-369, but it may take a further decline of a few hundred points in the Dow Jones Index to lift gold prices much higher," said Jeff Singer, chief bullion trader at Imperial Bank in California.
"In the meantime, a lot of people are happy being short, with holiday jewelry demand over now and demand down in the rest of the world because of the dollar's strength," he said.
COMEX February gold ended up 20 cents at $370.80 an ounce, after trading in a $369.70-371.10 range on estimated total volume near the close of 31,000 lots.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $368.90/369.40, up from the London Thursday afternoon fix at $368.60, and the New York close Wednesday at $368.60/369.10.
